introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography, Paper 3 (0750), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: three and a quarter hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer ALL THE THREE QUESTIONS. Question ONE carries THIRTY-FOUR marks and the rest carry THIRTY-THREE marks each.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answer.

Calculators are allowed.

Materials required: Topographic map, Graph Paper and photograph.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) (i) Complete the table above by filling the missing values **(10 marks)**

(ii) Calculate the correlation between distance from the city centre and the intensity of noise pollution using the formula stated below: **(6 marks)**

$$
R_s = 1 - \frac{6\Sigma d^2}{n^3 - n}
$$

Where: Rs is the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, Σd² is the sum of difference squared, and n is the number of items.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Completing the table (10 marks).**

1. *Rank Distance* (largest distance = rank 1, as the printed ranks show: 340 = 1, 330 = 2, 300 = 5, 250 = 6, 100 = 9, 50 = 10). Missing: 320 = **3**, 310 = **4**, 200 = **7**, 150 = **8**.
2. *Rank Noise* (highest noise = rank 1): 10 dB = 1; the two values of 8 dB share ranks 2 and 3, so each gets (2 + 3)/2 = 2.5 (printed for S/N 4); 6 dB = 4; 4 dB = 5; the three values of 3 dB share ranks 6, 7 and 8, so each gets 7 (printed); 2 dB = 9; 1 dB = 10. Missing: S/N 2 = **2.5**, S/N 5 = **5**, S/N 6 = **9**, S/N 10 = **10**.
3. *Difference d = Rank Distance - Rank Noise* (the printed values confirm the order, e.g. S/N 2: 9 - 2.5 = 6.5). Missing: S/N 1 = 10 - 1 = **9**; S/N 4 = 7 - 2.5 = **4.5**; S/N 8 = 3 - 7 = **-4**; S/N 9 = 2 - 7 = **-5**.
4. *d² = (difference) squared*: 81; 42.25; 16; 20.25; 1; 16; 9; 16; 25; 81.
5. *Total* of the last column: Σd² = 81 + 42.25 + 16 + 20.25 + 1 + 16 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 81 = **307.5**. Check: the d column adds up to 0 (9 + 6.5 + 4 + 4.5 + 1 - 4 - 3 - 4 - 5 - 9 = 0).

| S/N | Distance (n) | Noise level (dB) | Rank Distance | Rank Noise | d | d² |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 50 | 10 | 10 | 1 | **9** | **81** |
| 2 | 100 | 8 | 9 | **2.5** | 6.5 | **42.25** |
| 3 | 150 | 6 | **8** | 4 | 4 | **16** |
| 4 | 200 | 8 | **7** | 2.5 | **4.5** | 20.25 |
| 5 | 250 | 4 | 6 | **5** | 1 | **1** |
| 6 | 300 | 2 | 5 | **9** | -4 | **16** |
| 7 | 310 | 3 | **4** | 7 | -3 | 9 |
| 8 | 320 | 3 | **3** | 7 | **-4** | 16 |
| 9 | 330 | 3 | 2 | 7 | **-5** | **25** |
| 10 | 340 | 1 | 1 | **10** | -9 | **81** |
| **Total** |  |  |  |  | 0 | **Σd² = 307.5** |

(The sheet prints Σd² = 307; the exact sum of its own column is 307.5. Both values give the same coefficient to two decimal places, see below, so a candidate who uses 307 is not penalised.) Marks: about 0.5 mark per correct missing cell (19 cells), with the method (rank 1 = largest value, shared ranks averaged) shown.

**(ii) Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (6 marks).**

Formula (1 mark): $R_s = 1 - \dfrac{6\Sigma d^2}{n^3 - n}$, with $n = 10$ pairs of values, so $n^3 - n = 1000 - 10 = 990$ (1 mark).

Substitution and calculation (2 marks):

$$
R_s = 1 - \frac{6 \times 307.5}{990} = 1 - \frac{1845}{990} = 1 - 1.86 = -0.86
$$

(With the printed value 307: $1 - 1842/990 = -0.86$.)

Interpretation (2 marks):
- $R_s = -0.86$ is close to -1: there is a **strong negative (inverse) correlation**. The farther one is from the city centre, the lower the noise level; noise pollution is greatest near the centre, where traffic, industries, markets and crowds are concentrated, and it decreases with distance as sources become fewer, the sound spreads out and open spaces and vegetation absorb it.
- Significance: with $n = 10$, the usual tables of Spearman's coefficient give critical values of about 0.65 (5 % level) and 0.79 (1 % level); since $|-0.86|$ is larger than both, the relationship is statistically significant and is very unlikely to be due to chance. Remember that the data are hypothetical, only ten observations are used and some values are tied, and that a correlation does not by itself prove a cause.

| S/N Road | Number of passengers |

![fig-1](gce-al-geography-2026-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_2_fig_1.png)

*Outline map of Cameroon for Question 2. b) (i) Set B (separate sheet insert).*

(i) Using the map of Cameroon provided, construct a flow map/chart to represent the data. Use a scale of 1mm to represent 50,000 passengers to determine the thickness of the flow lines. Show all the steps of data processing. Where there are decimals, round the decimals to the nearest whole number. **(13 marks)**

(ii) Plot a simple bar graph to represent the data graphically. Let 1cm represents 50,000 passengers. **(2 marks)**

(iii) Comment on ONE merit and ONE demerit of the flow line technique of data representation. **(2 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The flow map (13 marks).**

*Step 1 - data processing (6 marks, 1 per town).* Width of each flow line (mm) = number of passengers / 50,000, rounded to the nearest whole number:

| Road | Passengers | Calculation | Exact width | Width drawn |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Yaounde - Douala | 600,000 | 600,000 / 50,000 | 12 | **12 mm** |
| Yaounde - Bafoussam | 150,000 | 150,000 / 50,000 | 3 | **3 mm** |
| Yaounde - Buea | 50,000 | 50,000 / 50,000 | 1 | **1 mm** |
| Yaounde - Bamenda | 80,000 | 80,000 / 50,000 | 1.6 | **2 mm** |
| Yaounde - Bertoua | 40,000 | 40,000 / 50,000 | 0.8 | **1 mm** |
| Yaounde - Ngaoundere | 100,000 | 100,000 / 50,000 | 2 | **2 mm** |

(The total traffic is 1,020,000 passengers; Douala alone takes about 59 %.)

*Step 2 - drawing (5 marks).*
1. On the outline map of Cameroon (set B), mark Yaounde as the common starting point and the six destination towns, which are already plotted (Douala, Bafoussam, Buea, Bamenda, Bertoua, Ngaoundere); Maroua, Garoua and Ebolowa carry no flow.
2. With a ruler, draw a straight line from Yaounde to each town. Each line has a constant width equal to the width in the table (use a ruler and two parallel lines, and shade the strip). The Douala line (12 mm) is the widest, the Bertoua and Buea lines (1 mm) the thinnest.
3. Keep the lines separate where they leave Yaounde, and do not cover the names of the towns.

*Step 3 - presentation (2 marks).* Give a title ("Flow map of road passenger traffic from Yaounde to selected towns, 2020"), a key (scale: 1 mm = 50,000 passengers, with one or two sample lines), the names of the towns, the source, and, if possible, a north arrow.

![fig-2](gce-al-geography-2026-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_2_fig_2.png)

*Model flow map drawn on the outline map. The line widths are drawn at 3 pixels per mm of the exam scale to fit the page (the real map needs the true widths: 12 mm for Douala, and so on).*

**(ii) The bar graph (2 marks).** One cm represents 50,000 passengers, so the bars are 12 cm (Douala), 3 cm (Bafoussam), 1 cm (Buea), 1.6 cm (Bamenda), 0.8 cm (Bertoua) and 2 cm (Ngaoundere) high (1 mark for the correct heights; no rounding is asked here). Draw the bars of equal width, separated by equal gaps, standing on a horizontal axis that carries the six roads, with a vertical axis scaled in cm (0 to 12) and labelled "Number of passengers (1 cm = 50,000)"; give a title (1 mark). The largest bar (12 cm) fits on an A4 sheet of graph paper. Bars may also be arranged in descending order.

![fig-3](gce-al-geography-2026-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_2_fig_3.png)

**(iii) One merit and one demerit (2 marks, 1 each).**
- *Merit:* the width of the line is proportional to the volume, so the map shows the direction, the origin and destination, and the size of the movement at a glance; it combines the location (map) with the quantity, and it shows clearly that the Yaounde - Douala axis dominates the traffic.
- *Demerit:* where several flows are large or start from the same point, the wide lines overlap and make the map crowded and hard to read (for example Douala and Buea); it takes time to calculate the widths and to draw them accurately, very small flows (less than 1 mm) are hard to draw, exact values are hard to read, and a straight line does not show the real road route.
